Bischoff: The Life & Art of an American Master, The Irvine Museum, 2010, p. 167, illustrated. | | Franz Bischoff first visited California—off the tail of a Michigan winter—at the turn of the 20th Century. By 1900, he had operated a successful China painting studio in the Greater Detroit area for two decades and recently become an American citizen. In the exuberance of his new status, the new century, and a glorious new climate, Bischoff fell in love with California quickly. He made the leap to greener pastures by 1906, moving his family to Southern California to start the next chapter of his career. | | Bischoff settled in Lincoln Park in South Pasadena where he established himself within the Arroyo Seco and Los Angeles art communities. This cohort included leading landscape painters of his day such as Hanson Puthuff, Benjamin C. Brown, Elmer and Marion Wachtel, and William Wendt. | | Bischoff's move to California marks a clear shift in his career, broadening his scope from still life to landscape painting, naturalism to Impressionism, studio to plein air, object to easel painting, and artistic production to artistic creation. | | At this time, California plein air painting was à la mode and championed by the leading art critic of this period, Antony Anderson of the Los Angeles Times. Anderson and Puthuff founded the Art Students' League of Los Angeles which 'would contribute greatly to the establishment of a progressive art tradition in Southern California.' 1 This specific cultural moment, along with Bischoff's personal trajectory, led Bischoff to find inspiration in his natural surroundings for nearly three decades. | | Picking Poppies, Pasadena dates to around 1910 when Bischoff became involved with the nascent California Art Club. He had also just built a new home and studio in South Pasadena that allowed him to hold public exhibitions very close to the views that inspired him. | | The present work brilliantly captures the floral and landscape subjects that inspired Bischoff along with the artistic and social history of his time. While the work is both a landscape and genre scene, Bischoff exhibits his mastery in Impressionist technique, conveying the movement and immediacy of this fleeting moment. Loose and dappled brushwork capture the ephemeral nature of California golden poppies and wildflowers, and color-laden strokes applied alla prima sculpt form into being. Capturing natural light conditions are solidly an Impressionist concern, and the painting skillfully conveys the diffused light of tree shade on the woman in the foreground and California's characteristic high-contrast, clear light on the women behind her. | | By the same token, the work shows a Modernist self-awareness of art history as a discipline (and the artist's place in it) by referencing the figural compositions of several canonical works as Jean-Francois Millet's, Des glaneuses, 1857, Édouard Manet's, Le déjeuner sur l'herbe, 1862-63, and Peter-Paul Ruben's, The Three Graces, 1630-35. Seen from this position, it is no coincidence that Henri Matisse's, La Danse, 1910—a work that echoes yet breaks from historical precedent—was created around the same time. | | The present work likely depicts the locale of Altadena near North Lake Avenue. Altadena's poppy fields were legendary—one field was so vibrant it was called La Sabanilla de San Pascual (The Altar Cloth of San Pasqual) by Spanish sailors who saw it from the coast. By the turn of the 20th Century, with the advent of modern transportation, these poppy fields became a tourist attraction, accessible by carriage and railway. | | Picking Poppies, Pasadena serves not only as a visual reminder of the fleeting pleasures of everyday life, but also as an important historic record of Altadena, particularly in light of conservation and wildfire recovery efforts today such as The Great Altadena Poppy Project. | | 1 J. Stern, Franz A. Bischoff: The Life & Art of an American Master, The Irvine Museum, 2010, p. 47.

provenance: Estate of the artist. | Elizabeth C. Hall, Belvedere, California, from the above. | Private collection, Belvedere, California. | Montgomery Gallery, San Francisco, California. | Private collection, Arizona. | Private collection, Northern California. | | Exhibited | Oakland, Oakland Art Gallery, Fourth Annual Exhibition of the Society of Six, 1926. | Montgomery Gallery, San Francisco, California's Society of Six, no date, no. 35. | | Literature | H.C. Dungan, Oakland Tribune, 'Artists and their Work,' April 4, 1926, p. 6-S, illustrated. | Montgomery Gallery, California's Society of Six, exhibition catalogue, San Francisco, no date, illustrated. | | Selden Gile and the Society of Six crafted a unique vision of California with the help of each other and the influence of several radical art movements. Modeled in part on the Group of Seven in Canada, the Society of Six spent over a decade in close contact and much longer sporadically gathering. The gregarious Gile was the driving force behind the Society of Six. He set the aesthetic standards that espoused color and guided the group with the strength of his personality, physical energy, and warm hospitality. With his high-energy and a sturdy build, he had a capacity for long hiking trips and outdoor, plein-air painting that he pursued passionately. He shared his house with several aspiring artists (like August Gay) and held dinners in a raucous atmosphere. Liberally seasoned with garlic and well lubricated with alcohol, the group critiqued and inspired one another. The avant-garde put in sporadic arrivals on the West Coast and when it did, the Six drank it up like one of Gile's home-brews. | | Stylistically, the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition (PPIE) was a transformative influence on the Six. For Gile, there is a palpable shift in style from the early teens through his mature pictures. In The Society of Six: California Colorists, Nancy Boas explains that this shift was in part a reaction to seeing the PPIE works: "After [the exhibition], the Six began applying loose, expressive brushstrokes of varying sizes, using the stroke as an element in its own right...Thus they abandoned the careful finish encouraged in academic work and attempted to reveal their own individuality and spontaneity in the paint surface itself. Combined with heavy impasto in some places and with unpainted areas of the canvas showing through in others, these brushstrokes create a purposeful sketchiness. Now sketchiness became a means of capturing a fleeting moment." 1 Building upon this shifted framework the 1923 exhibition of Contemporary French Art pushed the Society of Six to new heights of color and spontaneity. The fauves "wild beasts" were on view including Henri Matisse, Andre Derain and Maurice Vlaminck. The French critic Louis Vauxcelles applied the label to Matisse and Derain's works in a 1905 exhibition, and it grew to apply the artists themselves. | | The evolution of the Six shifted importantly with the start of their shared exhibitions in 1923. In Clapp's 1923 manifesto for the Society of Six, he concludes in part: In other words, we are not trying to illustrate a thought or write a catalogue, but to produce a joy through the use of the eyes...we have felt, and desire that others may also feel. Clapp—the theorist of the group—would come in for some reproach from his rough-and-tumble friends, as recounted by Siegriest in a 1972 interview: What the hell you writing all this crap down for... Get to painting and quite friggin around. Despite their criticisms, Clapp was speaking truthfully about an underlying goal of the Six. The French influence did not go unnoticed by critics of the time, Josephine Bentham in the Oakland Post Enquirer in March of 1923 referred to the Six as the Latin Quarter Comrades of the East Bay. Terry St. John observed in his 1972 book Society of Six that the turning point for Gile (and Von Eichman) was 1926 when they shifted to a more broadly Fauvist-influenced painting style.2 | | To understand the radical nature of these paintings it is helpful to read H.C. Dungan's review of the show in April of 1926 of the Oakland Tribune where he cautions those who attend that "you should have brought along your amber-tinted glasses, but not having them you will have to get used to the color. There's plenty of it; rich, pure, and let us add, Glorious. Dungan's choice of the word glorious was a preview of the praise he would lavish on the present lot in his review. "'Glorious Hill' by Selden C. Gile one of the outstanding canvases at the Society of Six exhibition at the Oakland Art Gallery. It is a fine example of color harmony and must be seen in the original to be appreciated." 3 | | The contrasts in color and form from the water to the arks to the hills and sky above proved an irresistible subject to Gile. He revisited it in numerous paintings and in 1927 moved north to Tiburon and later to adjacent Belvedere Island. The foreground of Glorious Hills is composed with subdued colors; Gile uses realistic greens and browns albeit with choppy brushwork. The arks and pilings come in for an altogether different treatment. The fauve's love of pure color from the tube is evident in the vibrant reds, pure yellows and saturated blues. All this action in color and form in the arks is framed below by water with long gestural swirls in the white and green and as Dungan calls it "too blue" water. The arks are framed above by the orange and green hills stepping up to the sky with the occasional darker green daubs of trees and maroon shadows. The sky has more of the pure blue, particularly on the edges; however much of it is overlayed with glorious white and butter yellow clouds with some subtle pink hints. The scale of the work serves to emphasize the different skills Gile can bring to bear on one composition. Dungan notes "that's a good sized canvas, but it is much bigger in art than it is in square inches." 4 | | 1 N. Boas, The Society of Six: California Colorists, San Francisco, 1988, pp. 80-81. | 2 T. St. John, Society of Six: William Clapp, August Gay, Selden Gile, Maurice Logan, Louis Siegriest, Bernard Von Eichman, Oakland, 1972. | 3 H.C. Dungan, Oakland Tribune, 'Artists and their Work,' April 4, 1926, pg. S6 | 4 ibid Dugan, p.S6.

March 15-27, 1920, and elsewhere. | (Likely) Los Angeles, Los Angeles Museum of History Science and Art, Eleventh Annual Exhibition of the California Arts Club, October-November, 1920. | (Likely) Pasadena, Shakespeare Club, May 1921. | | Literature | Suzanne Muchnic, 'Art and Architecture: Setting the Stage for a California Scene,' The Los Angeles Times, April 1, 2001, p. 252, illustrated. | | When the group of artists now known as the Impressionists held their first exhibition in 1874 it was largely met with poor reviews and general distaste. Over a decade later however, art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel successfully reintroduced this once avant-garde movement to American audiences at an 1886 exhibition with more positive acclaim. From it developed American Impressionism, a light and airy style of painting that captured predominantly leisure pursuits. This movement varied in both style and subject from the dark and rigid manner of the Academic tradition that preceded it and the grittier urban scenes of the Ashcan movement that followed. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries regional manifestations of American Impressionism appeared in Boston, New York, Connecticut and as far West as California, each with their own nuanced interpretations of the French style. Guy Rose's Incoming Fog, La Jolla exemplifies this intersection of French, American, and ultimately California Impressionism in a visual evolution of plein-air painting. | | Born in 1867 on a family ranch in the San Gabriel Valley, Guy Rose is one of few West Coast artists of this period native to California. As the son of a wealthy landowner, Rose experienced a relatively privileged upbringing that afforded him the opportunity to travel. Following his graduation from Los Angeles High School in 1885, Rose first ventured north to San Francisco where he trained at the California School of Design under Virgil Williams and Emil Carlsen. From there he went on to study at the Académie Julian in Paris in 1888. At both institutions, he followed a rigorous curriculum that prioritized time spent in the studio drawing and practicing form. During weekends and summer breaks however, he scheduled visits to the nearby countryside to practice painting directly from nature. It was here that Rose was first exposed to Impressionism and captivated by a style of painting that would gradually inform the rest of his career. | | Rose was not the only American who found the French countryside and Giverny in particular appealing. Together with artists like Frederick Frieseke, Lawton Parker and Richard Miller, they were dubbed 'The Giverny Group' by critics.1 This new generation of expatriate artists continued to embrace the original tenets of Impressionism first championed by Claude Monet - short broken brushstrokes, pure unblended color and emphasis on the effects of light. | | An early example of Monet's fascination with both color and light can be seen in his 1867 work The Regatta at Saint-Adresse (The Metropolitan Museum of Art 51.30.4). Here well-dressed beachgoers spend a leisurely afternoon watching a fleet of sail boats in the harbor town of Le Havre as billowing clouds form above. With a subtle gradation in the tan pigments, Monet perfectly distinguishes the wet versus dry areas of the shoreline. Rose would go on to use a similar effect in Incoming Fog with mossy greens delineating the water level on the rocky outcrop. Another striking similarity between the two works is the use of rapid brushwork to portray depth of field. Just as Monet's scene articulates distinct zones of shallow, moderate, and deep water, Rose's composition is similarly structured, with long fluid strokes beyond the break and shorter rapid ones in the foreground to simulate aerated water tossed about by waves. While Rose never painted the sea during his time abroad, it is clear Monet's influence continued to have an impact on his later works. | | By the time the prodigal son returned to California after more than a decade overseas, he brought with him a vast firsthand knowledge of what was happening in the art world in both Europe as well as on the East Coast. While Giverny continued to host Americans until the outbreak of World War I, artist colonies were simultaneously beginning to develop stateside in areas like Cos Cob, Old Lyme, Shinnecock, Carmel and Laguna Beach. Unlike the East Coast however, California benefited from year-round sunshine making its coastlines the ideal setting for Rose to continue building on the practice of plein-air painting as he reacquainted himself with his home state. | | Early on critics saw merit in Rose's rendering of the sea with Antony Anderson of the Los Angeles Times noting, "Rose had never painted the sea till a year ago, and when he gazed upon the Pacific it must have been with a new and 'wild surmise' for he immediately sat himself down to paint it - and discovered he had come into his own. Luckily for him and thrice luckily for us." 2 From here on, Rose's oeuvre oscillates between images of intense glare and subtle fog as he pushes the boundaries of Impressionism to focus purely on atmospheric effects. In the present lot, fog slowly begins to encroach on the scene from the left side of the composition as the sea and sky blur into one. Meanwhile, the horizon line on the right side of the canvas remains in perfect clarity, at least for the time being as the title would suggest. The duality of the composition captures Rose's mastery of the thick marine layer of Lifting Fog (sold at Bonhams in 2024) and the shimmering brilliant light of Off Point Lobos (sold at Bonhams in 2022). | | Guy Rose remains one of the most distinguished American Impressionists to come out of California, with a forthcoming 2027 retrospective of his work at the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento attesting to the continued interest in his contribution to plein-air painting. | | 1'Luminism of Giverny,' New York Evening Post, December 20, 1910, p.9. | 2 Antony Anderson, The Los Angeles Times, February 20, 1916.

Hansen first started producing cowboy compositions in 1913 after a friend took him to a rodeo in Salinas just east of Monterey. 1 Although he had been exposed to Western Art from an earlier age through his father, Herman Wendleborg Hansen, the majority of his own artistic output up to that point largely focused on seafaring culture. Often marked by rain-soaked decks, turbulent seas and weathered fishermen, these maritime scenes still alluded to the frontier with overlapping themes of hard labor and untamed nature. By 1930, Hansen reintroduced the rodeo subject in a Los Angeles exhibition, which stood out among his marines and led a reviewer to declare that Hansen had "gone western."2 | | Hansen's rodeo scenes are not only a departure from his standard subject matter but his use of color as well. His maritime scenes are typically rendered in deep monochrome shades of ultramarine or indigo, primarily cool tones that mirror the cold isolation of life at sea. In contrast to the more somber mood evoked by a cool palette, the present lot shares the same warmer tones as Cowboy Sport and First Feel of Leather (each sold at Bonhams) that capture the liveliness and animation of sport. Here Hansen uses shades of maroon, salmon, orange and vermillion to render various ten-gallon hats, chaps and bandanas. Long shadows are cast in tones of deep forest green. A dab of purple on one rider's spur balances the various shades of mustard that make up the dusty haze, while another in turquoise brings some semblance of focus into the otherwise frenzied scene. Hansen further obscures the spectacle with a cropped composition that enhances the action taking place within the corral. | | Despite verging on abstraction, the finished product is a direct result of Hansen's accomplishments as a draftsman. Each stroke is placed with intention to mimic the line work he perfected in etchings like Cowboy Sport and Over the Top. From the weight of a rider suspended mid-air to the musculature of a bucking bronco, Hansen manages to retain the underlying structures and forms of his subjects in a feat of organized chaos that captures the Spirit of the Rodeo. | | 1 Scott A. Harlow & Co., Big Game: An Exhibition of Paintings by Carl Rungius, April 1921. | | Literature | (Probably) New York Times, Art Exhibitions of Paintings, April 10, 1921, Section D, p. 81. | | This painting will be included in the forthcoming Carl Rungius Catalogue Raisonné, directed by Dr. Adam Duncan Harris (an independent project of the National Museum of Wildlife Art). | | Carl Rungius was arguably the most influential American wildlife painter, not only by virtue of his artistic skill but through his education and advocacy. He brought an up-close and personal view of wildlife to the public at-large—particularly with the diorama murals he painted for the American Museum of Natural History in New York—that made a compelling case for the value of land conservation in the 20th Century. | | Rungius was born in a provincial district of present-day Berlin. He developed an interest in art and hunting from a young age, which culminated in attending the Berlin Academy of Arts. Rungius 'was lauded as a painter of moose before he'd ever laid eyes on the living, breathing beast' so when he was invited by his uncle, Dr. Clemens Fulda of New York, to hunt moose with him in Maine, he jumped at the chance. 1 | | Though Rungius was unsuccessful in his first season of moose hunting, this trip in the Fall of 1894—his first to North America—set him on his path. Determined to capture a moose the following Fall, he stayed on for another year with his uncle. | | Rungius made two important connections in 1895—the first was with William Hornaday, a leading figure in America's conservation movement and later Director of the New York Zoological Society; and the second was with Ira Dodge, an outfitter from Wyoming's Wind River Country. | | Hornaday saw a life-sized head-and-shoulders portrait of a bull moose which Rungius had painted after specimens he studied at the American Museum of Natural History and a local taxidermy studio and remarked that 'It looked as if a section with a wild animal in it had been cut out of the Maine woods and framed as an exhibit from the workshop of nature.' 2 The two men became fast friends, and Hornaday introduced him to other prominent sportsmen in New York that became his most influential supporters, including the figurehead of the Bull Moose Party, Theodore Roosevelt. | | Dodge met Rungius at New York's first Sportsman's Show at Madison Square Garden and invited him to hunt for Big Game through the Wind River Range that year. Rungius fell in love with the American West from this trip to Dodge's Box-R Ranch and decided to stay in America permanently. For his remaining years, Rungius split his time between New York City in the Winter; and Wind River, Maine, New Brunswick and Banff in the Summer and Fall. 3 | | Rungius successfully hunted his first moose in 1898, just south of Dodge's dude ranch which Roosevelt had also visited. He continued to develop his fidelity to moose from trekking in New Brunswick, earning a reputation as 'the Rembrandt of the moose.' 4 | | Moose were the most enduring subjects for Rungius, and he captured them across four of the five regions he visited annually. Rungius's painterly approach toward them evolved over time, starting from a highly naturalistic and detailed technique, as seen in Lost Timber, circa 1900 (National Museum of Wildlife Art, JL 2000.116) toward a lively Impressionistic technique, as seen in At the Pond. | | 1 T.
